slides.title: Laws that shape frontend code
slides.summary: Privacy, payment, accessibility and product-security rules all have concrete requirements for the UI.
body: Compliance isn't only a legal team's job. Many requirements land directly in frontend code: what you store, what you load, and how you ask for consent.
<mark>Collect the least personal data you need, and don't load trackers before the user agrees where consent is required.</mark>

body.note: This is an engineering overview, not legal advice. Check what applies to your product and users with your legal team.

cells.text: Ask before non-essential cookies and trackers
“Do not sell or share”; honour Global Privacy Control
Clear consent notices; rules phase in to 2027
Script inventory + tamper detection on payment pages

figure.alt: A sketch of a shop web page with five areas, each labelled with the rules that apply. The cookie banner: GDPR and ePrivacy require consent before non-essential cookies and trackers, with reject as easy as accept. Analytics and ad scripts: CCPA/CPRA and other US state laws require honouring Global Privacy Control; India's DPDP rules require consent notices. The checkout payment page: PCI DSS 4.0.1 requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1, mandatory since March 2025, require an inventory of every script with a justification and detection of unauthorised changes to scripts and headers. The sign-up form: data minimisation, and no personal data in URLs or logs. The whole page: the European Accessibility Act, in force since June 2025, and the ADA require accessible UI, typically WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 AA.

slides.title: Privacy and payment pages in practice
slides.summary: Consent before tracking, no personal data in URLs or logs, and a controlled, monitored set of scripts on payment pages.

ul: Consent first: load analytics and ad scripts only after opt-in where required, and make “Reject” as easy as “Accept”.
Honour Global Privacy Control: read navigator.globalPrivacyControl or the Sec-GPC header and treat it as an opt-out.
Keep personal data out of URLs: URLs end up in logs, analytics and Referer headers.
Scrub logs and error reports before they leave the browser: emails, tokens, form values.

body.h: PCI DSS 4.0.1 on payment pages (mandatory since 31 March 2025)

ul: 6.4.3: keep an inventory of every script on payment pages, with a reason for each, and confirm each is authorised and unmodified.
11.6.1: detect unauthorised changes to those scripts and to security headers, at least weekly.

body: <mark>The simplest way to shrink PCI scope is a hosted payment page or the provider's iframe fields, plus a strict CSP and SRI on whatever remains.</mark>
